title: Vanadium superconducting microwave resonators on silicon wafers
authors: Y. Fujita, Y. Urade, Y. Hibino, M. Tsujimoto, K. Inomata, G. Fujii, W. Mizubayashi
abstract: Understanding the correlation between material properties and microwave losses in superconducting films is a crucial subject for developing low-loss materials for quantum circuits. We focus on vanadium (V) as a novel material for superconducting quantum devices and discuss loss in V films in relation to their structural properties. Using a sputtering method, we grow four V-film structures on (001)-oriented Si wafers, employing Nb and Ta as the buffer and capping layer materials, respectively: Nb/V/Ta, Nb/V, V/Ta, and V. X-ray diffraction and atomic force microscopy reveal that the V films grown on the Nb buffer layers have higher uniformity of lattice orientation and smaller grain size than that directly grown on the Si wafer. Coplanar waveguide resonators are fabricated from the four V-film structures, and averaged photon number ($\langle n_{\rm ph} \rangle$) dependences of internal quality factor ($Q_{\rm int}$) are obtained by performing microwave measurements. By analyzing the obtained $Q_{\rm int}$ vs $\langle n_{\rm ph} \rangle$, it is found that loss at the V surface is dominated by $\langle n_{\rm ph} \rangle$-independent non-two-level-system (non-TLS) losses, which can be mitigated by introducing the Ta capping layer. Furthermore, the V films on the Nb buffer layers exhibit lower $Q_{\rm int}$ in the $\langle n_{\rm ph} \rangle$ range from 10$^{0}$ to 10$^{6}$ and higher non-TLS loss than that directly grown on Si wafers, even though the former has higher lattice-orientation uniformity than the latter. Origins of these trends might be relevant to V oxides, of which presence at surfaces and grain boundaries in bulk regions in the V resonators is suggested by energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and/or V hydrides.
summary: This experimental study investigates how modifying the structure of Vanadium superconducting films using buffer and capping layers affects their microwave loss in resonators. By correlating structural data with $Q_{	ext{int}}$ measurements, the authors pinpoint non-TLS losses originating from surface oxides or hydrides as a key limitation for quantum circuit development.
main_problem: The study aims to understand how material properties, particularly surface chemistry and structural quality, influence microwave losses in superconducting Vanadium (V) films used in quantum circuits.
main_result: While buffer layers improve crystal structure, the presence of V oxides or hydrides at grain boundaries appears to be a dominant source of non-TLS loss, which can be mitigated by capping layers like Tantalum (Ta).
method: The research combines structural characterization (XRD, AFM) with electrical and microwave measurements ($Q_{int}$ vs. $\langle n_{	ext{ph}} angle$) and surface analysis (XPS, EDS).
model_or_system: The physical system is a superconducting resonator built from V films on Si wafers, modified by Nb buffer layers and Ta capping layers. Loss mechanisms are analyzed using the photon-number dependence of the internal quality factor ($Q_{int}$).
key_observables: Internal quality factor ($Q_{	ext{int}}$), non-TLS loss ($\delta_{	ext{other}}$), lattice orientation uniformity (XRD FWHM), and surface oxidation states (XPS).
important_parameters: Photon number ($\langle n_{	ext{ph}} angle$), temperature (down to 10 mK), film thickness, and buffer/capping layer materials (Nb, Ta).
main_assumptions: The microwave loss can be modeled by separating contributions into Two-Level System (TLS) losses and photon-number-independent non-TLS losses.
figures_summary: Figures show XRD profiles confirming lattice coherence enhancement with Nb buffers; AFM images detail surface roughness changes; $Q_{int}$ vs. $\langle n_{	ext{ph}} angle$ plots analyze loss mechanisms, and XPS spectra map out various V and Ta oxide states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from structural characterization (Nb buffer effect) to electrical property analysis ($	ext{Tc}$, $	ext{RRR}$), then focuses on microwave loss modeling ($Q_{int}$ vs. $\langle n_{	ext{ph}} angle$), and finally correlates these losses with detailed surface chemistry findings (oxides/hydrides).
why_interesting: The work directly addresses the practical challenge of material engineering for quantum devices by linking microscopic defects (oxides, grain boundaries) to macroscopic performance metrics ($Q_{int}$), which is crucial for designing reliable superconducting circuits.
